chunks.text: Fraud awareness and prevention at the branch
headingPath: Fraud awareness and prevention at the branch

chunks.text: Branch staff are the first line of defense against social engineering, identity theft, and unauthorized fund transfers. This policy outlines common fraud patterns in Pakistan banking, mandatory verification rules, and immediate escalation protocols.

Fraudsters frequently call or visit branches claiming to be regulatory officials, head office auditors, or IT support personnel asking for passwords, system overrides, or customer PINs.

Rule: Head office and IT staff will never ask a branch officer for customer credentials, one-time passwords (OTPs), or system passwords over the phone. Any such request must be treated as an attempt to compromise the bank and reported immediately to the Information Security Incident Desk.

A common scheme involves a fraudster obtaining a customer's CNIC copy and attempting to change the registered mobile number at the counter. Once the number is updated, the fraudster registers for mobile banking and intercepts OTPs to empty accounts.

Rule: Mobile number updates require:

1. Physical presence of the account holder with their original CNIC.
2. Biometric thumb impression verification matched via NADRA.
3. Confirmation of the previous three transactions on the account.
A mobile number change can never be processed on behalf of a third party, family member, or through an authority letter without written sign-off from the Branch Manager.
headingPath: Pattern 2: Digital banking and OTP diversion

chunks.text:
Altered cheques typically target amounts and beneficiary names. Signs of alteration include:

- Inconsistent ink shade or pen stroke thickness.
- Chemical washing marks around the payee line or amount box.
- Differences between the written words and numerical figures.

Rule: For any clearing or counter cheque exceeding five hundred thousand rupees (PKR 500,000), telephone confirmation with the drawer using the registered contact number is mandatory before passing the instrument. Never use contact numbers handwritten on the back of the cheque.
headingPath: Pattern 3: Cheque cloning and altered instruments

chunks.text:
When fraud is suspected:

1. Do not alert the suspicious individual at the counter.
2. Inform the Branch Operations Manager using the designated quiet signal.
3. Freeze the affected account immediately in the core banking system to prevent outgoing transfers.
4. Log an incident report with the Compliance and Anti-Money Laundering unit within two hours.

outline.title: Guarding the Branch: Fraud Awareness and Prevention
outline.summary: A story-driven learning journey that trains branch staff to recognize and stop common fraud patterns in Pakistani banking, including social engineering, SIM/mobile number swap fraud, cheque alteration, and proper escalation protocols when fraud is suspected.

chapters.title: The Imposter Callers
chapters.arcBeat: New staff member encounters suspicious phone calls and visits at the branch, learning to spot impersonation attempts before any damage is done.

missions.title: The Fake IT Officer
missions.objective: Identify a social engineering attempt from a caller posing as IT support asking for a password.

missions.title: Raise the Alarm Quietly
missions.objective: Practice the correct reporting steps when a credential request is suspicious.

chapters.title: The SIM Swap Trap

missions.title: Spot the Forgery
missions.objective: Examine a cheque for signs of chemical washing, ink inconsistency, and word-figure mismatches.

missions.title: The Branch Under Threat
missions.objective: Handle a complex, multi-signal fraud scenario combining impersonation, mobile number change request, and a suspicious cheque, applying all learned protocols correctly.

concepts.summary: Fraudsters impersonate regulators, head office auditors, or IT staff to trick branch officers into revealing passwords, OTPs, or system overrides. No legitimate head office or IT request will ever ask for these over the phone.

concepts.name: Verifying Mobile Number Update Requests
concepts.summary: Mobile number changes are a common vector for account takeover fraud. Strict rules require the account holder's physical presence, original CNIC, NADRA biometric verification, and confirmation of the last three transactions before any change is processed.

concepts.name: Identifying Signs of Cheque Alteration
concepts.summary: Altered cheques often show inconsistent ink, chemical washing marks near the payee or amount, and mismatches between written words and numeric figures. Staff must inspect cheques carefully for these signs.

concepts.name: Telephone Verification for High-Value Cheques
concepts.nameUr: بڑی رقم کے چیک کی ٹیلی فون تصدیق
concepts.summary: For cheques exceeding PKR 500,000, staff must call the drawer using the registered contact number on file before honoring the cheque. Numbers written on the back of the cheque must never be used.

concepts.name: Fraud Escalation Protocol
concepts.nameUr: فراڈ کی صورت میں انتظامی کارروائی کا طریقہ کار
concepts.summary: When fraud is suspected, staff must avoid alerting the suspect, quietly inform the Branch Operations Manager, freeze the account in the core banking system, and log an incident report with Compliance and AML within two hours.

roleplay.goal: Trick the branch staff into revealing their system password by posing as urgent IT support.
openers: Hi, this is IT support, we need your password to fix a server issue right now.
Listen, the whole branch system will lock if you don't give me your login immediately.
I'm calling from Head Office IT, your manager already approved this, just give me the password.

behaviors.text: Caller creates false urgency about a system lockout to pressure quick compliance.
Caller claims to be from Head Office or IT to sound authoritative.
Caller directly asks for the system password over the phone.
Caller threatens to involve management if the staff member refuses.

callbacks.prompt: Can IT or Head Office ever ask you for your password over the phone?
keyPoints: No, this is never allowed as per the rule.
Such a request should be treated as a compromise attempt.

callbacks.prompt: What should you do right after refusing a suspicious password request?
keyPoints: Report it immediately to the Information Security Incident Desk.
Do not delay or ignore the incident.

pack.objective: Identify a social engineering attempt from a caller posing as IT support asking for a password.

hints: Think about what Head Office IT is actually allowed to ask for over the phone.
Remember the rule about credentials, OTPs, and passwords never being requested by phone.
The correct action combines refusing the request with reporting it immediately.
questions.prompt: The caller claims to be IT and demands your password. What do you do?

label.en: Refuse and report to Information Security Incident Desk
label.ur: انکار کریں اور انفارمیشن سیکیورٹی انسیڈنٹ ڈیسک کو رپورٹ کریں
label.urLatn: Inkar karein aur Information Security Incident Desk ko report karein

options.consequence: You protect the bank and alert the right team immediately.

label.en: Give the password since he sounds official
label.ur: چونکہ وہ سرکاری لگتا ہے، پاسورڈ دے دیں
label.urLatn: Chunke woh sarkari lagta hai, password de dein

options.consequence: You may have just handed a fraudster access to bank systems.

label.en: Say you'll call back later and hang up without reporting
label.ur: کہیں کہ بعد میں کال کریں گے اور بغیر رپورٹ کیے فون بند کر دیں
label.urLatn: Kahein ke baad mein call karenge aur baghair report kiye phone band kar dein

options.consequence: Delaying without reporting leaves the attempt unrecorded and risks recurrence.

label.en: Ask your manager if this is normal before refusing
label.ur: انکار کرنے سے پہلے مینیجر سے پوچھیں کہ کیا یہ معمول ہے
label.urLatn: Inkar karne se pehle manager se poochein ke kya yeh mamool hai

options.consequence: This wastes time; the rule is clear that IT never asks for passwords by phone.

variants.standard: The caller claims to be IT and demands your password. What do you do?
variants.foundation: A caller says he is IT and asks for your password. What is your first move?

questions.workedExample: A caller claims to be IT and asks for your password. You refuse, explain the rule, and report the call to the Information Security Incident Desk right away.

hints: Escalation threats are a common pressure tactic used by fraudsters.
The rule about not sharing passwords does not change under pressure.
The safe response always pairs refusal with reporting.
questions.prompt: The caller escalates, threatening to involve your manager if you don't share the password. What's the right response?

label.en: Stay firm, refuse, and report the call
label.ur: ثابت قدم رہیں، انکار کریں اور کال رپورٹ کریں
label.urLatn: Sabit qadam rahein, inkar karein aur call report karein

options.consequence: Pressure tactics don't change the rule; you correctly refuse and report.

label.en: Give the password to avoid trouble with management
label.ur: انتظامیہ سے مسئلہ بچنے کے لیے پاسورڈ دے دیں
label.urLatn: Intezamia se masla bachne ke liye password de dein

options.consequence: Fear of escalation is exactly what fraudsters exploit to get credentials.

label.en: Hang up and do nothing further
label.ur: فون بند کر دیں اور مزید کچھ نہ کریں
label.urLatn: Phone band kar dein aur mazeed kuch na karein

options.consequence: Hanging up without reporting misses the chance to alert the bank to a real threat.
